newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt will outperform deficit target - minister.
newsitem.headline: Egypt will outperform deficit target - minister.

text.p: The Egyptian government expects to outperform the deficit target in its 1997/8 budget, as it has also done in the current year ending on June 30, an economics minister told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday.

Youssef Boutros-Ghali, minister of state for economic affairs, also said the government was comfortable with the current exchange rate and did not believe that a cheaper Egyptian pound would do much to stimulate exports.
The minister said the level of the budgeted 1997/8 deficit as a proportion of GDP did not imply any change in fiscal policy. Parliament approved the budget in late May.
The new target is 1.2 percent of GDP, compared to an achievement of about 0.8 percent in the current year. The original target for 1996/7 was 1.5 percent.
"It is not a significant movement. It does not denote any particular stand in policy," Boutros-Ghali said.

"We overperformed on the previous target and it is very likely that we will overperform next year (1997/8). I don't see the difference between the two numbers (1.2 and 0.8 percent) as statistically important," he added.
Asked if the government might eventually ease fiscal restraints for the sake of some extra growth, as some Egyptian economists propose, he said: "Not at the moment."

He said he expected the economy to grow by between 5.5 and 5.7 percent in 1997/8, slightly higher than in 1996/7. "This year it will be around five, five point something percent. It's not going to disappoint us," he added.
On the government's longstanding but largely ineffective drive to promote Egyptian exports, he said this was now President Hosni Mubarak's top economic priority.

A high-level committee on exports will meet in July to look at a range of proposals, he said. These cover the tax and customs treatment of exporters, procedures at ports and airports, international marketing strategies and financial services such as credit guarantees and long-term financing.
But the government would not tamper with the Egyptian pound, which has been stable in the range of 3.30 and 3.40 to the dollar for six years despite relatively high inflation.

"Our export problems are not problems of price... They are problems of competitiveness in terms of export infrastructure -- marketing, quality, consistency in delivery, consistency in quality, timeliness in delivery -- all the issues that come with a long tradition of exporting," he said.
"In terms of price, we surveyed our exporters and there is no problem in cost or price competition," he added.
Asked if this meant the government was happy with the current exchange rate, he said it was.
The minister confirmed that the government would carry out a new round of import duty cuts in July, as part of an IMF-approved programme to liberalise trade.
He did not say how steep they would be or if they would include vehicles, excluded from the last round of cuts in 1996.
The minister said he thought the Egyptian economic reform had found its stride and the stock market, an important element as the main channel for privatisation, was maturing.

"We see a broadening of the investor base and in the stock market we see a deepening. It's becoming less volatile. For the inexperienced, they see a slightly quiet period in the market as worrisome. I see it as maturity," he said.
$1 = 3.395 pounds
